parts.label: a
parts.display_text: Sketch a labelled p–V cycle for a diesel-engine model: adiabatic compression from V₀ to V₀/20; isobaric expansion to V₀/10; adiabatic expansion to V₀; cooling at constant volume back to the starting state.

answer.text: The first curve rises steeply to the left; the second is horizontal to the right; the third curves down to the right; the fourth is vertical downward at V₀. The cycle is clockwise and encloses the net work output.

source.collection_label: Tim Kirk · Oxford 2003 · 1998 question reproductions
source.title: 1998 IB Physics questions reproduced in Tim Kirk's study guide

parts.label: b
parts.display_text: A fixed amount of gas initially has pressure 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, temperature 27 °C and volume V₀. It is compressed to V₀/20, with final pressure 6.6 × 10⁶ Pa. Calculate its final temperature.

answer.text: For a fixed amount, PV/T is constant. T₂ = 300 × (6.6 × 10⁶/1.0 × 10⁵)/20 = 990 K.

source.collection_label: Tim Kirk · Oxford 2003 · 1998 question reproductions
source.title: 1998 IB Physics questions reproduced in Tim Kirk's study guide

parts.label: c
parts.display_text: For the four-stage diesel cycle described in (a), identify when work is done on the gas, when work is done by the gas, and when combustion supplies thermal energy.

answer.text: Work is done on the gas during stage 1. It is done by the gas during stages 2 and 3. Heat from combustion is supplied during the approximately isobaric stage 2. No volume work occurs in stage 4.

source.collection_label: Tim Kirk · Oxford 2003 · 1998 question reproductions
source.title: 1998 IB Physics questions reproduced in Tim Kirk's study guide

parts.label: d
parts.display_text: Explain how the second law of thermodynamics limits the efficiency of this diesel-engine cycle.

answer.text: A cyclic engine must reject some heat to a colder reservoir; it cannot convert all absorbed heat to work. The total entropy change of the engine and surroundings cannot be negative.

answer.text: Official answer C; editorial worked explanation: A Carnot cycle contains two isothermal processes joined by two adiabatic processes. On a P–V diagram for an ideal gas, both expansion curves fall as volume increases, and an adiabat is steeper than an isotherm through the same region. Only option C has the two falling isotherms connected by two steeper falling adiabats in the required closed cycle.
